summary_md: Zeileis (JSS 16(9), 2006; read as the sandwich package vignette) recasts heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC) and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) covariance estimation as a modular sandwich S = (1/n) B M B, where the bread B is the inverse Hessian and the meat M is the variance of the empirical estimating functions. R generics bread(), estfun(), meat(), meatHC() and meatHAC() let one computation serve lm, glm, survreg and other models. Two illustrations show what the correction does. In a Poisson fit to simulated negative-binomial data (n = 250), the naive z for I(x^2) is -2.12 (p = .034); with the sandwich it is -1.35 (p = .18). In a probit on Fair's affairs data (n = 601), age moves from p = .033 to p = .051. The author's own caveat carries the most weight: sandwich errors help only if the point estimates stay consistent, they cost power when the model is right, and the package does no inference itself. For Paul's systems the paper is a method source, not evidence. The Mentat sector-growth study hand-codes the same estimators in base R: HC1 (meat as an outer product with the n/(n-k) factor) as a reference-only error, CR1 and two-way cluster errors, and, in SEATS-W, a Bartlett-weighted Newey-West HAC at 2, 4 and 8 week lags kept secondary with no p-value. The way the system is built already follows the paper's caveat, since primary inference comes from wild-cluster and block bootstraps. The paper's HC meat also ignores cluster dependence, which the study handles separately with CR1. One real gap: HC1 and CR1 are cross-checked against statsmodels in a test, but no comparable second-path check was found for the hand-coded HAC (for example against sandwich::NeweyWest), so under DE-062 those HAC numbers stay UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: HC sandwich = (1/n) B M B with meat as the outer product of estimating functions and an optional n/(n-k) adjustment (Eq. 10, p.6); sandwich errors are useful only if estimates stay consistent and lose power under correct specification; probit age p moves .033 to .051 (n = 601).
bearings.system_side: OLS with sector fixed effects reports HC1 = (n/df) A X'uu'X A as a reference-only error. Primary inference is a wild cluster restricted bootstrap with CR1, plus a two-way cluster sensitivity. This matches the paper's estimator and respects its caveat that HC is not a stand-alone inference rule.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The design is linear, so the paper's HC0/HC1 theory transfers directly. The HC meat assumes independent observations; within-sector dependence needs CR1 (sgs_estimate.R:44), which the paper does not cover. Statsmodels cross-checks HC1 and the cluster errors at tests/test_estimate.py:44-45.

bearings.paper_claim: The HAC meat is a weighted sum of lagged estimating-function cross-products (Eq. 11, p.7) behind the NeweyWest()/kernHAC() wrappers. The paper reports no coverage study and names Kiefer-Vogelsang fixed-b testing as an alternative to sandwich-based restriction tests (p.14).
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W computes Newey-West HAC errors by hand: Bartlett weights 1 - l/(L+1) at L = 2, 4 and 8 weeks within cycle, with n/(n-p). They are reported as secondary with no p-value. Primary inference is the moving-block bootstrap, and the code notes that a Senate result significant under HAC lost Holm support under the bootstrap.
bearings.transfer_conditions: With about 17 weeks per cycle and one election, HAC asymptotics are weak, so keeping HAC secondary (sgs_seats.R:71-77) fits the paper's limits. No second-path check of this hand-rolled HAC against sandwich::NeweyWest was found.

gaps_exposed: The hand-coded Newey-West HAC in sgs_seats.R:391-400 has no second-path reproduction such as sandwich::NeweyWest(lag = L, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = TRUE). HC1 and CR1 do have statsmodels checks at tests/test_estimate.py:44-45. Under DE-062 the HAC figures stay UNVERIFIED.

No coverage or size simulation exists for HC1 or HAC at the study's sample sizes (sector-year panels; about 17 weeks per cycle). The paper offers none either, so the reference errors carry no finite-sample guarantee.

The paper's HC meat assumes independent rows. Any Mentat or Melange regression quoting HC1 on panel data without clustering would understate uncertainty. The growth study avoids this, but the rule is not stated system-wide.
flags: Paper is a software and method paper with no substantive political finding; it does not bear on SNA, LDA or reciprocity rules.
Paper figures (z -2.12 to -1.35; p .033 to .051) come from one simulated dataset (n = 250) and one cross-section (n = 601). They illustrate the estimator and do not validate it.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated-bibliography entry and no markup for this work (n_annots 0), so there is no takeaway to compare against. The built system already follows the paper's central caveat: HC1 and HAC are kept as reference or secondary errors, and bootstraps carry inference. This fits Paul's directives to present regressions as R summary() output with a bootstrap and to put trend over significance.

related.why: Zeileis 2004 (JSS 11(10)) is the linear-model HC/HAC predecessor this paper generalizes to any estimating-function model. It holds the HC2-HC4 and HAC weight details this paper only cites.

The later sandwich vignette adds clustered (CR) covariances to the same bread/meat framework. This is the estimator family the growth study actually uses for primary inference (CR1, two-way clustering).
